newsitem.title: ROMANIA: CEAUSESCU'S PLAYBOY HEIR DIES IN VIENNA HOSPITAL.
newsitem.headline: CEAUSESCU'S PLAYBOY HEIR DIES IN VIENNA HOSPITAL.

text.p: Nicu Ceausescu, the hard-drinking, womanising youngest son of Romania's late Stalinist dictator, died in a Vienna hospital on Thursday, where he was being treated for serious liver disease.

Nicu, 45, was flown to Austria a week ago for specialised surgery in an attempt to save his life, after Romanian doctors admitted they lacked the necessary medical and surgical equipment to deal with his condition.
His elder brother Valentin, said he was shocked by the news and could not immediately comment.

Nicu was known as a womaniser who squandered vast sums of public money at the gambling tables of Las Vegas and other casino towns. His flamboyant reputation symbolised what many saw as the moral bankruptcy of his father's dictatorship.
Nicu was rushed to the Bucharest university hospital on September 14 with internal bleeding, caused by what doctors said was a varicose oesophagus and acute liver cirrhosis.
Nicu's critical health condition, coupled with a shortage of modern medical equipment, prevented Romanian doctors from performing vital surgery to prepare him for a liver transplant.
He was flown to Vienna General Hospital last week where doctors were expected to bring his bleeding under control. He was believed to be on waiting list for the transplant when he died.
"Mr Ceausescu died at 6 a.m. (local time, 0400 GMT) this morning," a hospital spokeswoman said.
His girlfriend of several years, Dana Radu, had accompanied him to the Vienna hospital.
Nicu was the youngest of three children of late communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu and his wife, Elena.
A violent revolution in December 1989 ousted the Ceausescus after a ruthless 24-year rule. They were shot by firing squad on Christmas Day.

The communist nomenclatura, including the Ceausescu children, enjoyed luxurious lifestyles while the mass of the population lived in dire poverty with food rationing, power blackouts and lack of heating.
Meat, dairy products and other staples had become scarce as Ceausecu tried to pay back foreign debt.

Nicu, a physicist, was head of the Communist Party's youth wing and was posted to Sibiu in the early 1980s, where local people remember him for trying to resist his father's severe economic belt-tightening policies.
Valentin, a nuclear physicist, and his sister Zoe, a mathematician, have kept a low profile since they were released from detention in 1990.
Groomed to be his father's successor, Nicu was Communist Party boss in the central county of Sibiu when the 1989 revolution broke out.
He was sentenced to 20 years in jail for mass murder after ordering the repression of protests in his Sibiu fiefdom during the 1989 revolt.

He had always denied the mass-murder charge and accused the post-communist authorities of making him a scapegoat. That charge was later dropped and only a five-year sentence for illegal gun possession was upheld.
By the time of his release on health grounds in November 1992, he had served half of the jail term -- enough for parole based on good behaviour.
Romanian prosecutors earlier this year closed the file on a criminal probe launched against the Ceausescu children in the wake of the anti-communist revolution.

They were cleared of charges of undermining the national economy -- charges on which their parents were killed -- by using their privileged position to exploit assets of the now defunct Communist Party.
A foreign travel ban on the children was also lifted.
Many Romanians now harbour ambivalent feelings about the Ceausescu era and their fall.

Living standards are lower and many people believe the true story of the 1989 revolution -- which many see as a coup d'etat by former communists who have held power ever since -- has yet to be told. REUTER
